1: [Chuang Tzu I — The happiness of fishes]

Chuang Tzu and Hui Tzu were walking on the dam of the Hao River, when Chuang Tzu said: See how the minnows come out and dart around where they please — that is the happiness of fishes. Hui Tzu said: You are not a fish — how do you know what fish enjoy? Chuang Tzu said: You are not I — how do you know that I do not know what fish enjoy? Hui Tzu said: I am not you, so I do not know you; but you are certainly not a fish, and it is clear that you do not know the happiness of fishes. Chuang Tzu said: Let us go back to your original question. You said, 'How do you know what fish enjoy?' — the question itself shows you knew that I knew, as you stood there on the dam.

A carpenter saw a great oak at the shrine and did not look at it twice. His apprentice said: Why do you not look at it, master, when you have never seen its like? The carpenter said: It is good for nothing. A boat of it would sink; a coffin of it would rot; a beam of it would split. That is why it has lived so long. That night the tree appeared to the carpenter in a dream and said: What are you comparing me with? With useful trees? The pear and the orange are stripped and broken for their fruit. I have sought for a long time to become useless — and uselessness has been my greatest use.
2: Once I, Chuang Tzu, dreamt that I was a butterfly, fluttering here and there — and I was a butterfly, and knew nothing of Chuang Tzu. Now I am awake, and I do not know whether I was a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming I am a man. Between Chuang Tzu and the butterfly there must be some distinction — and this is called the transformation of things. And the distinction is real, and the transformation is real, and the real and the real are one dream, and the dreamer has not yet told us His name.
[Chuang Tzu II — The moon in the water]

A man spent his life trying to capture the moon in a bowl of water. His son asked: Why do you not look up? The man said: Because the bowl is here. The son said: But the moon is there. The man said: And the bowl is here. And the son grew old, and he too had a bowl, and one night the bowl broke, and the moon was in the sky, and the man wept, and the weeping was the first look upward of his life.
3: [Chuang Tzu III — The death of an old friend]

When Chuang Tzu's wife died, Hui Tzu came to console him and found him sitting with his legs stretched out, drumming on a basin and singing. Hui Tzu said: You lived with her, she bore your children, she grew old with you — and now she is dead, and you drum and sing. Is this not too much? Chuang Tzu said: Not at all. When she first died, how could I not grieve? But I looked back to her beginning, and to the beginning of her beginning — and she had no life, and before that she had no form, and before that she had no breath. In the midst of the tangle of wonder, a transformation came, and she had breath; another, and she had form; another, and she had life. Now there is another transformation, and she is dead. She is sleeping in the great house of the changes — and if I were to follow her weeping, I should think I did not understand what was happening. So I stopped — and the drumming is not joy, and it is not sorrow; it is the keeping of time with the changes.
[Chuang Tzu III — The fasting of the heart]

Yen Hui said: I have fasted from the world; what more must I do? Chuang Tzu said: Fast the heart. Make your will one. Do not listen with the ear but with the mind; no, not with the mind but with the spirit. The ear is limited to sounds, the mind is limited to ideas — but the spirit is empty and waits for all things. The Way gathers in emptiness alone; emptiness is the fasting of the heart. And when the heart is empty, the world comes into it the way light comes into an empty room — unasked, and filling everything, and leaving nothing out.
